steps.title: One handshake, three jobs
text: TLS 1.3 is the lock behind the web, and this lesson walks through its {{term:handshake}} one message at a time.
The handshake does three jobs. It makes a shared key (lesson 3). It lets the client check who the server is (lesson 4). Then it switches on the lock for the real data (lesson 1).
This run uses the hybrid key exchange, X25519 and ML-KEM together. A client and a server talk over loopback, and the client sends one line and gets it back.
Built to show the parts. Do not copy.

steps.title: ClientHello: the client offers
text: The client speaks first. The ClientHello lists the lock suites it can use, the groups it can use for key exchange, and a key share for the group it expects to win.
Open the inspector. The hybrid share holds an ML-KEM key and an X25519 share side by side, 1,216 bytes in all. The message travels in the clear, so an eavesdropper reads it.
Try it: swap the client's X25519 share on the way out. The two sides will end up with different keys, and the first sealed record will not open.

claims.text: The ClientHello carries the client's offered cipher suites and key shares.
claims.source: RFC 8446, section 4.1.2 (Client Hello) and section 4.2.8 (Key Share)

claims.text: In this lab the hybrid client share is 1,216 bytes and the hybrid server share is 1,120 bytes.
After a replaced client key share, the two sides hold different keys, so the first sealed record fails the AEAD tag check before any Finished arrives.
claims.source: docs/lessons-4-5-names.md, section 'Three corrections to ux-design.md section 8', item 1 (branch feat/s3)

steps.title: ServerHello: the server chooses
text: The server answers with its choice of suite and its half of the key exchange. This is the last message that travels in the clear.
The client checks a special value in the server's random bytes. It is the downgrade sentinel, and the check passes here.
Try it: flip one byte of the ML-KEM ciphertext in the ServerHello. ML-KEM reports no error for a damaged ciphertext. The client simply derives a different key, and a later check catches the mismatch.

tryIt.label: Flip one byte of the ML-KEM ciphertext

claims.text: All handshake messages after the ServerHello are encrypted.
A TLS 1.3 client that receives a ServerHello indicating TLS 1.2 or below must check the last 8 bytes of the server random for the downgrade sentinel.
ML-KEM gives no error for a damaged ciphertext (implicit rejection), and in the lab the damage shows up as a failed AEAD tag on the first sealed record.
claims.source: FIPS 203, Algorithm 18 (ML-KEM.Decaps_internal); docs/lessons-4-5-names.md, corrections item 1 (branch feat/s3)

steps.title: A ladder of secrets
text: Both sides now hold the key-exchange secrets. From them each side builds a ladder of keys, rung by rung, with a hash-based key function.
Open the secrets panel. The rungs come in order: the handshake secret first, then the traffic secrets for the handshake, then the master secret and the traffic secrets for the real data.
Each rung comes from the one above it plus a hash of the messages so far. Change an earlier message and every rung below it changes too.

claims.text: TLS 1.3 derives its keys in stages with HKDF, mixing in the transcript hash of the messages so far.

steps.title: The lock switches on
text: Watch the next message. At the instant the handshake keys go in, readable blue bytes turn into scrambled amber ones.
From here on, every message in that direction is sealed with an AEAD, the lock-plus-tag from lesson 1.

claims.text: In TLS 1.3 all ciphers are modeled as authenticated encryption with associated data (AEAD).

steps.title: EncryptedExtensions: the first sealed message
text: The server sends its settings in a sealed record called EncryptedExtensions. An eavesdropper can no longer read what the server says.
Try it: switch to the eavesdropper view. The arrows stay and the bytes turn to noise.

steps.title: A sealed record breaks on one flipped byte
text: The client opens the record and checks its tag. On the normal run the tag matches, so the lab emits no event for it. Only a failure shows up as a check.
Try it: flip one byte of the sealed record. The tag no longer fits, the check named AEAD tag fails, and the client ends the talk.

tryIt.label: Flip one byte of the sealed record

steps.title: Certificate: who is the server?
text: The server now sends its certificate and the signature that proves it holds the key. Lesson 4 walked through the five checks the client makes here.
In this lab all five pass: the chain, the signature, the dates, the name, and the CertificateVerify proof.
Notice who is proving what. Only the server proves itself in this run. The server did not ask the client for a certificate.

claims.text: A server that authenticates with a certificate may optionally request a certificate from the client (CertificateRequest), and a client sends a Certificate message only if the server asked for one.

steps.title: Server Finished: nothing was changed
text: The server ends its flight with Finished. It is a seal over the whole handshake, made with a key that only the two sides can compute.

If an attacker changed any earlier message, the two sides would disagree about the handshake, and the seal would not fit. This also protects the offer the client made, so an attacker cannot quietly weaken it.
Try it: flip one byte of the server's Finished data before it is sealed. The client's check named Finished verify_data fails.

tryIt.label: Flip one byte of the server's Finished

claims.text: Finished is essential for providing authentication of the handshake and of the computed keys, and recipients must verify its contents.

steps.title: Client Finished, then the data flows
text: The client answers with its own Finished. The server checks it the same way.
A client Finished shows that the client holds the same keys. It is not a login. The server still does not know who this client is.

A server that wants to know can ask for a certificate with a CertificateRequest. The client then signs the handshake with its own key, as the server did. Lesson 10 shows a client proving itself, with a signed challenge and a token.

claims.text: Clients must send a CertificateVerify whenever they authenticate with a certificate, so a client can prove itself the way a server does.

steps.title: Real data under real keys
text: The client sends its one line as ApplicationData. It travels under the application keys from the bottom of the ladder.
Switch between the Endpoints and Eavesdropper views. The endpoints read a line of text. The eavesdropper sees noise.

steps.title: A record that never ends
text: The client closes the talk with an alert. A close alert is a polite goodbye, and both sides then stop.
One more attack: make a record claim to be 256 bytes longer than it is. The receiver waits for bytes that never come. After up to 30 seconds it gives up with the check named read deadline.
In step mode the clock restarts whenever the engine holds an event for you, so you can read as long as you like.

tryIt.label: Make a record claim to be longer than it is

claims.text: TLS endpoints close a connection with a closure alert; in the lab a record with an inflated length waits up to 30 seconds and ends with the read deadline check.
claims.source: RFC 8446, section 6.1 (Closure Alerts); docs/lessons-4-5-names.md, corrections item 3 (branch feat/s3)

steps.title: What the hybrid covers
text: The hybrid protects the key exchange. An attacker who records this talk today cannot read it after quantum computers arrive, as long as ML-KEM stays secure.
Certificates stay classical. The signatures on the server's card use classical math, so a future quantum attacker could forge them. The hybrid does not change that.
Built to show the parts. Do not copy.

claims.text: The hybrid protects the key exchange only. Certificates stay classical.
